claim: A CloudWatch Logs subscription gives you a real-time feed of log events delivered to services such as an Amazon Kinesis stream, an Amazon Data Firehose stream or AWS Lambda for custom processing, analysis or loading to other systems.
q: How do you stream CloudWatch log events to Kinesis, Firehose or Lambda as they arrive?
v: a real-time feed of log events
an Amazon Data Firehose stream, or AWS Lambda
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions

You can use subscriptions to get access to a real-time feed of log events from CloudWatch Logs and have it delivered to other services such as an Amazon Kinesis stream, an Amazon Data Firehose stream, or AWS Lambda for custom processing, analysis, or loading to other systems.

claim: You can use a CloudWatch Logs subscription to stream log data in near real time to an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster.
q: Can CloudWatch Logs stream log data to Amazon OpenSearch Service?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions
You can also use a CloudWatch Logs subscription to stream log data in near real time to an Amazon OpenSearch Service cluster.

claim: Log events are sent to the receiving resource of a subscription soon after being ingested, usually in less than three minutes.
q: How quickly does a subscription filter deliver log events?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions
Log events are sent to the receiving resource soon after being ingested, usually less than three minutes.

claim: When log events are sent to the receiving service of a subscription, they are base64 encoded and compressed with the gzip format.
q: In what format does a subscription filter deliver log events?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions
When log events are sent to the receiving service, they are base64 encoded and compressed with the gzip format.

claim: You can create subscriptions at the account level and at the log group level; each account can have one account-level subscription filter per Region, and each log group can have up to five subscription filters.
q: At which levels can you create CloudWatch Logs subscription filters?
sc: per Region (account level), per log group
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions

You can create subscriptions at the account level and at the log group level. Each account can have one account-level subscription filter per Region. Each log group can have up to five subscription filters associated with it.

claim: An account-level subscription policy can include a subset of the log groups in the account and can work with Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, AWS Lambda or Amazon Data Firehose.
q: Which destinations can an account-level subscription policy use?
v: a subset of log groups in the account
AWS Lambda, or Amazon Data Firehose
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/SubscriptionFilters-AccountLevel

You can set an account-level subscription policy that includes a subset of log groups in the account. The account subscription policy can work with Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, AWS Lambda, or Amazon Data Firehose.

claim: If the destination of a subscription returns a retryable error such as throttling or an HTTP 5xx error, CloudWatch Logs keeps retrying delivery for up to 24 hours.
q: How long does CloudWatch Logs retry delivery to a subscription destination after a retryable error?
v: retry delivery for up to 24 hours
retryable error such as a throttling exception
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions

If the destination service returns a retryable error such as a throttling exception or a retryable service exception (HTTP 5xx for example), CloudWatch Logs continues to retry delivery for up to 24 hours.

claim: Subscription filters ensure at least one time delivery of events, while duplicate events may occasionally occur.
q: Can a subscription filter deliver the same log event twice?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions
Subscription filters ensure at least one time delivery of events, while duplicate events may occasionally occur.

claim: For a cross-account subscription, the log group and the destination must be in the same AWS Region, but the AWS resource that the destination points to can be in a different Region.
q: Must a subscription destination be in the same Region as the log group?
v: must be in the same AWS Region
can be located in a different Region
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CrossAccountSubscriptions
The log group and the destination must be in the same AWS Region. However, the AWS resource that the destination points to can be located in a different Region.

claim: Subscription filters can cause an infinite recursive loop that can lead to a large increase in ingestion billing if not addressed; AWS recommends excluding the log groups that ingest data from the subscription delivery workflow.
q: What billing risk do account-level subscription filters carry?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/SubscriptionFilters-AccountLevel

There is a risk of causing an infinite recursive loop with subscription filters that can lead to a large increase in ingestion billing if not addressed. To mitigate this risk, we recommend that you use selection criteria in your account-level subscription filters to exclude log groups that ingest log data from resources that are part of the subscription delivery workflow.

claim: AWS recommends that you do not regularly export logs to Amazon S3 as a way to continuously archive them; for that use case it recommends subscriptions instead.
q: Should you use CloudWatch Logs export tasks to archive logs continuously?
v: don't regularly export to Amazon S3
we instead recommend that you use subscriptions
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/S3Export
We recommend that you don't regularly export to Amazon S3 as a way to continuously archive your logs. For that use case, we instead recommend that you use subscriptions.

claim: Log data can take up to 12 hours to become available for export to Amazon S3, and export tasks time out after 24 hours.
q: How long until CloudWatch Logs data can be exported to S3, and when does an export task time out?
v: up to 12 hours to become available for export
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/S3Export
Log data can take up to 12 hours to become available for export. Export tasks time out after 24 hours.

claim: You can export log data to S3 buckets encrypted with AES-256 or SSE-KMS; exporting to buckets encrypted with DSSE-KMS is not supported.
q: Which S3 bucket encryption types work with a CloudWatch Logs export task?
v: encrypted with AES-256 or with SSE-KMS
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/S3Export
You can export to S3 buckets that are encrypted with AES-256 or with SSE-KMS. Exporting to buckets encrypted with DSSE-KMS is not supported.

claim: You can export log data from log groups to an Amazon S3 bucket in the same account or a different account, including a bucket with S3 Object Lock enabled with a retention period.
q: Can a CloudWatch Logs export task write to another account's S3 bucket or an Object Lock bucket?
v: same account or a different account
S3 Object Lock enabled with a retention period
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/S3Export
You can export to an S3 bucket in the same account or a different account.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/S3Export
Export log data to S3 buckets that have S3 Object Lock enabled with a retention period

claim: You can keep exported log files in your S3 bucket and define Amazon S3 lifecycle rules to archive or delete them automatically.
q: How do you archive or expire exported CloudWatch log files?
v: archive or delete exported files automatically
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/S3Export
You can store the exported files in your S3 bucket and define Amazon S3 lifecycle rules to archive or delete exported files automatically.

claim: With CloudWatch Logs Insights you can interactively search and analyze your log data in CloudWatch Logs, using a purpose-built query language, OpenSearch PPL or OpenSearch SQL.
q: Which CloudWatch Logs feature lets you run interactive queries on log data?
v: interactively search and analyze your log data
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/AnalyzingLogData
With CloudWatch Logs Insights, you can interactively search and analyze your log data in Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/AnalyzingLogData
CloudWatch Logs Insights supports 3 query languages that you can use for your queries:

claim: CloudWatch Logs Insights cannot access log events with timestamps that pre-date the creation time of the log group.
q: Can Logs Insights query events older than the log group's creation time?
v: pre-date the creation time of the log group
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/AnalyzingLogData
CloudWatch Logs Insights can't access log events with timestamps that pre-date the creation time of the log group.

claim: In a monitoring account set up for CloudWatch cross-account observability, you can run CloudWatch Logs Insights queries on log groups in the linked source accounts, including one query across log groups in different accounts.
q: Can one Logs Insights query cover log groups from several accounts?
v: queries multiple log groups located in different accounts
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/AnalyzingLogData

If you are signed in to an account set up as a monitoring account in CloudWatch cross-account observability, you can run CloudWatch Logs Insights queries on log groups in source accounts linked to this monitoring account. You can run a query that queries multiple log groups located in different accounts.

claim: CloudWatch Logs Live Tail lets you troubleshoot incidents by viewing a streaming list of new log events as they are ingested, and you can view, filter and highlight them in near real time.
q: Which CloudWatch Logs feature shows new log events as they arrive?
v: streaming list of new log events
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatchLogs_LiveTail

CloudWatch Logs Live Tail helps you quickly troubleshoot incidents by viewing a streaming list of new log events as they are ingested. You can view, filter, and highlight ingested logs in near real time, helping you to detect and resolve issues quickly.

claim: Live Tail sessions incur costs by session usage time, per minute.
q: How is CloudWatch Logs Live Tail charged?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatchLogs_LiveTail
Live Tail sessions incur costs by session usage time, per minute.

claim: A log anomaly detector scans the log events ingested into a log group and finds anomalies automatically, using machine learning and pattern recognition to establish baselines of typical log content.
q: How does CloudWatch Logs find unusual log patterns automatically?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/LogsAnomalyDetection

A log anomaly detector scans the log events ingested into a log group and finds anomalies in the log data automatically. Anomaly detection uses machine-learning and pattern recognition to establish baselines of typical log content.

claim: Logs transformation and enrichment lets you normalize your logs into a consistent, context-rich format at the time of ingestion into CloudWatch Logs.
q: Can CloudWatch Logs reshape log events as they are ingested?
v: at the time of ingestion into CloudWatch Logs
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CloudWatch-Logs-Transformation
With logs transformation and enrichment, you can normalize all your logs in a consistent and context-rich format at the time of ingestion into CloudWatch Logs.

claim: Log Analytics is a unified console experience in CloudWatch Logs that brings together CloudWatch Logs Insights, Live Tail and Contributor Insights, and it is the default experience for analyzing logs in the CloudWatch Logs console.
q: What is CloudWatch Log Analytics?
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/LogAnalytics

Log Analytics is a unified console experience in Amazon CloudWatch Logs that brings together log analysis capabilities in one place. You can query and analyze log data with CloudWatch Logs Insights, stream logs in real time with Live Tail, and identify your top contributors with CloudWatch Contributor Insights. Log Analytics is the default experience for analyzing logs in the CloudWatch Logs console.

claim: Many AWS services publish logs only to CloudWatch Logs, while others use vended log delivery to send logs directly to Amazon S3 or Amazon Data Firehose.
q: Where can AWS services deliver their vended logs?
v: publish logs only to CloudWatch Logs
vended log delivery to send logs directly
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/AWS-logs-and-resource-policy
Many services publish logs only to CloudWatch Logs, but others use vended log delivery to send logs directly to Amazon Simple Storage Service or Amazon Data Firehose.

claim: Even when a service publishes logs directly to Amazon S3 or Firehose, CloudWatch delivery charges apply.
q: Are vended logs sent directly to S3 or Firehose free of CloudWatch charges?
v: publish logs directly to Amazon S3 or Firehose
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/AWS-logs-and-resource-policy
Even when you publish logs directly to Amazon S3 or Firehose, CloudWatch delivery charges apply.

claim: If a log group has no resource policy and the user setting up logging has the needed logs permissions, AWS automatically creates the resource policy that lets the service write logs when you begin sending the logs to CloudWatch Logs.
q: Who creates the log group resource policy for vended logs?
v: AWS automatically creates the following policy
log group currently does not have a resource policy
ev: docs/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/AWS-logs-infrastructure-CWL

If the log group currently does not have a resource policy, and the user setting up the logging has the `logs:PutResourcePolicy`, `logs:DescribeResourcePolicies`, and `logs:DescribeLogGroups` permissions for the log group, then AWS automatically creates the following policy for it when you begin sending the logs to CloudWatch Logs.
